issues.claim: Green Lanes was an old drovers' road for taking animals to London.
issues.problem: Stated as fact; sources only say it possibly began as a drovers' road.
issues.correct: Green Lanes 'possibly originated as a drovers' road along which cattle were walked from Hertfordshire to London.'
issues.suggested_text: The same name gave Haringey and Hornsey, three spellings of one old word. Green Lanes was probably an old drovers' road for taking cattle to London.

issues.claim: Both villages are now next to Heathrow Airport.
issues.problem: Harlington borders Heathrow, but Hayes lies further north, beyond Harlington and the M4; sources call the airport 'nearby', not next to Hayes.
issues.correct: Harlington adjoins the airport's northern edge; Hayes is a few kilometres north of it.
issues.suggested_text: Hayes comes from Old English hæs, brushwood. Harlington was recorded in 831 as Hygereding tun. Harlington now borders Heathrow Airport.

issues.claim: It was recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Hendun.
issues.problem: Hendun is the older, pre-Domesday form (10th-century charter). Domesday spells it Handone.
issues.correct: Hendun is earlier than Domesday; the 1086 Domesday form is Handone.
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded as Hendun before the Domesday Book of 1086. The station opened in 1923.

issues.claim: Highbury was the higher of two manors in the parish.
issues.problem: Islington parish had several manors (Barnsbury, Canonbury, Holloway, Highbury). Highbury was named for its hilltop site, above the lower manors.
issues.correct: A new manor house was built on a hill in 1271 and called Highbury; it looked down on the lower manors of Barnsbury, Canonbury and Holloway.
issues.suggested_text: Islington was recorded around 1000 as Gislandune. Highbury manor stood on a hill above the other manors of the parish. The Victoria line station opened in 1968.

issues.claim: The stream was a tributary of the River Fleet, long since buried.
issues.problem: In the 'hollow stream' explanation the stream is the River Fleet itself (its upper course). The tributary idea belongs to a different theory (Stow's 'Old Bourne'), which other historians doubt.
issues.correct: Holborn 'may derive from Middle English hol (hollow) and bourne (brook), referring to the River Fleet'.
issues.suggested_text: The stream was probably the River Fleet itself, long since buried. Londoners traditionally say 'Hoe-bun'.

issues.claim: 'Holloway' means the hollow way, a road worn deep into the ground.
issues.problem: Sources say the origin is disputed and that no documentary evidence supports either the 'hollow way' or the 'hallow' (pilgrim) explanation; the text states one as certain and ranks the other.
issues.correct: 'The origins of the name are disputed... No documentary evidence can be found to support either derivation.' 'Hollow way' is the more usual explanation.
issues.suggested_head: 'Holloway' probably means the hollow way, a road worn deep into the ground.
issues.suggested_text: Cattle on their way to London's markets wore the road down over centuries. Some think it was a 'hallowed way' for pilgrims instead.

issues.claim: St Andrew's Church still has the head of a bull with real horns on its east end.
issues.problem: The horns are metal, not real: found to be copper in 1824; stolen in 1999 and replaced in 2001.
issues.correct: A bull's head stands at the east end of the roof; its horns are copper (replacements since 2001).
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded in 1222. Nobody knows exactly why, but St Andrew's Church still has a bull's head with copper horns on its east end.

issues.claim: 'Kennington' means the farm of a man called Cena.
issues.problem: This is Mills's interpretation; sources also give a second explanation ('town of the King'). Missing hedge.
issues.correct: Mills: 'farmstead or estate associated with a man called Cēna'; another explanation is 'place/town of the King'.
issues.suggested_head: 'Kennington' probably means the farm of a man called Cena.

issues.problem: Wrong borough. The station is east of the High Road, which is the Camden side.
issues.correct: Local authority: London Borough of Camden.

issues.claim: His family had owned the land since at least the early 17th century, and he named the main road after himself.
issues.problem: The Ladbroke family's ownership is documented from the late 18th century (Richard Ladbroke, d. 1793), not the early 17th; James Weller inherited about 1821. No source says he named the road himself.
issues.correct: Richard Ladbroke owned the estate in the late 18th century; it passed to his nephew James Weller (who took the Ladbroke name) around 1821. The street is named after him.
issues.suggested_text: He inherited the land from his uncle around 1821, and the main road was named after him. The station opened in 1864 as Notting Hill.
